newsitem.title: USA: Pentagon said to ignore Gulf War chemical evidence.
newsitem.headline: Pentagon said to ignore Gulf War chemical evidence.

text.p: Members of Congress and U.S. servicemen who served in the Gulf War said on Tuesday that evidence of chemical agents had been detected during the conflict that could have damaged the troops' health.

"You are voices in the wilderness that no one has listened to," Representative Christopher Shays, R-Connecticut, told three servicemen who testified to his House of Representatives Government Reform and Oversight subcommittee.
He said earlier Pentagon denials about the presence of chemicals had "crumbled under the weight of reluctantly disclosed facts."

An army chemical warfare specialist, Sgt. George Grass, testified that equipment on board a chemical detection vehicle he commanded in Kuwait in Feburary 1991 repeatedly sounded alarms for nerve agents and other chemicals in the air ranging from minute traces to lethal concentrations.
Grass said the chemicals detected included nerve agents in minute amounts, the blistering agent "s-mustard" and benzene bromide.
He said the readings were taken in a minefield and at an Iraqi ammunition dump that contained boxes marked with skull and crossbones signs.

He said that although his superiors insisted that some readings were "false positive," the data had been printed out, the detection vehicles had been fully checked before use and their crews were well trained.
Other commanders of detection vehicles had since told him of making positive identification of chemical agents during the war, Grass said.
Army Maj. Michael Johnson, who served as a chemical weapons investigator in Kuwait, said he had no doubt that the detection equipment had functioned properly.

The subcommittee is looking into charges that toxic chemicals experienced by the troops might be responsible for what has become known as the Gulf War Syndrome -- a multitude of health problems that have afflicted the war veterans.

Several major studies have concluded that there is no single Gulf War Syndrome but two studies appear to show that more Gulf War veterans suffer the flu-like symptoms than soldiers who were not in the Gulf War.
Pentagon officials, while accepting that troops were exposed to at least some deadly chemicals, have said that there is no evidence it hurt them.

Testifying with Grass were Marine Maj. Lee Herbert, who blamed his health problems, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, also known as Lou Gehrig's disease, on low level chemical exposure over an extended period.

Independent Representative Bernard Sanders of Vermont charged there had been "an apparent cover-up" of exposure to chemicals and said that victims could have been treated if the problem had been known earlier.
"Now we know the 'all clear' came too soon," Shays said. He said there had been credible, verified detection of chemical nerve and blister agents in the Gulf War.
